p:cNvPr.descr: A cyclical illustration of how glucose transport works with GLUT4 transporters and insulin. An illustrated diagram showing how insulin and GLUT4 work to make glucose transport occur. There is a close-up of a cell, the inside of which is light pink, with the cell membrane mostly yellow in the center with blue edges on the top and bottom. The plasma membrane is labeled on the left. On the left is an insulin receptor, which is a small domed light pink protein extending up from the cell membrane. It traverses the membrane and secures with two blue club-shaped appendages. To the right are several vesicles, each representing a different point in the process of glucose transport. On the lower left is a gray text box reading, “ (1) Glucose transporters are “stored” within the cell in membrane vesicles.” To the right is a vesicle, which is a circle lined yellow with plasma membrane, and 4 blue clothespin-shaped proteins, which are the glucose transporters, attached to the edges of the vesicle. An arrow points up to show the upward movement of the vesicle to its right. To the left of the vesicle is the insulin receptor. A small red ball, representing insulin, bonds to the insulin receptor. Above the insulin receptor is a gray text box reading, “(2) When insulin interacts with its receptor, vesicles move to the surface and fuse with the plasma membrane, increasing the number of glucose transporters in the plasma membrane.” On the insulin receptor, the clublike blue appendages become active (shown by activity lines). A dashed arrow extends from the insulin receptor to the right, where there is a circled green triangle. Just below the triangle is an upward, right-curving arrow showing the migration of the vesicle up to the cell surface membrane. Here the vesicle becomes an indentation in the membrane and the glucose transporters are exposed on the cell surface. Three blue dots, representing glucose, are floating in the indentation, and one more has been picked up by the GLUT4 transporter. A fifth glucose is shown having been transported inside the cell. Outside the cell is an arrow pointing to the right, showing the movement of the GLUT4 transporters. They are now in a row on a flat portion of the membrane, with one holding a glucose and another glucose floating just above. A gray text box to the upper right reads, “(3) When insulin level drops, glucose transporters are removed from the plasma membrane by endocytosis, forming small vesicles.” To the right is another indentation, showing that the vesicle is beginning to form again. There are 3 molecules of glucose floating in the indentation. A down arrow shows the vesicle forming again inside the cell. A down and left arrow has a gray text box to the right that reads, “(4) The smaller vesicles fuse with a larger endosome.” To the left of this the small vesicle that just formed has fused with a large endosome, which is also lined with membrane and has 2 GLUT4 transporters as well. A text box to the left reads, “(5) Patches of the endosome enriched with glucose transporters bud off to become small vesicles, ready to return to the surface when insulin levels rise again.” A final left & up arrow points back to the initial vesicle.
